skyline.text: How a crowded street fed a world­wide pop­u­la­tion panic
Why tyranny makes peo­ple stop hav­ing chil­dren, from Poland to Russia
Five met­als, ten years, and a prophecy of doom un­done

masthead.footnote: *Human beings are the ultimate resource. Page 2

brief.head: Crowded, and rich
brief.text: Monaco is forty times as dense as Bangladesh and far richer, Amit Varma said, cit­ing Nicholas Eberstadt, who found no link be­tween den­sity and poverty. {#monaco}

brief.head: Children as insurance
brief.text: The poor have more chil­dren be­cause they see them as re­sources, Amit Varma said. High child mor­tal­ity made them in­sur­ance, yet the pat­tern per­sists as mor­tal­ity falls. {020-C06}

brief.head: Plague as policy
brief.text: Malthus wrote that in­stead of rec­om­mend­ing clean­li­ness to the poor, we should court the re­turn of the plague. For him, Amit Varma said, plague meant de­liv­er­ance. {020-J11}

brief.head: Any family will do
brief.text: Ajay Shah ar­gued that India should stop in­sist­ing only a fa­ther and mother can raise a child, and open up to sin­gle par­ents and oth­ers. {020-C14}

brief.head: Out on a bare branch
brief.text: The Chinese call them “bare branches”: young men who never learn a trade, earn an in­come or build a fam­ily. No gov­ern­ment dole, Ajay Shah said, can sub­sti­tute. {020-C15}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why people are an asset
lead.head: More mouths, more minds

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 20

body: As a school­boy in the era of the “Hum Do Hamare Do” slo­gan, Amit Varma was taught why India was poor: there were too many peo­ple. It sounded in­tu­itive. Only in adult­hood did he re­alise the op­po­site was true. {020-S01}
“That is a ca­nard that we were fed,” Varma said, and it angers him that most peo­ple still be­lieve it.
His an­swer fits in a phrase: peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs. More peo­ple, he said, mean big­ger net­works, more pos­i­tive-sum games and more trades that leave both sides bet­ter off.

The proof is where peo­ple choose to live. All of human his­tory, Varma said, is mi­gra­tion from sparse vil­lages to dense cities. People move from Bihar to Mumbai, not the other way round. {020-C02}
There is a moral point too: call­ing pop­u­la­tion a prob­lem, he ar­gued, means call­ing other peo­ple the prob­lem.
## Doom, post­poned

The pes­simism is old. In 1798 Thomas Robert Malthus ar­gued that re­sources grow arith­meti­cally and peo­ple ex­po­nen­tially, so star­va­tion must fol­low. In 1967 Paul Ehrlich’s *The Population Bomb* de­clared that the bat­tle to feed all of hu­man­ity was over.

Hundreds of mil­lions would starve in the 1970s and 1980s, Ehrlich pre­dicted. They did not. Such fore­casts project a curve into in­fin­ity, Varma said, but “any­one sta­tis­ti­cally knows that you can­not ex­trap­o­late a trend and as­sume that it will con­tinue for­ever.” {020-C05}
Ehrlich even bet on ris­ing re­source prices, and lost. He is still, Varma noted, a hero of the left, though “he has been wrong about ev­ery­thing in his life”.
## The state and the body

The idea had vic­tims. Reading from Coomi Kapoor’s *The Emergency*, Varma de­scribed Sanjay Gandhi’s ster­il­i­sa­tion drive: quo­tas for every dis­trict and of­fi­cer, salaries with­held, and po­lice fir­ing on vil­lagers who re­sisted.
Even if you think pop­u­la­tion is a prob­lem, he said, co­er­cive fam­ily plan­ning tells cit­i­zens that “you do not own your bod­ies”.

Ajay Shah com­pared three worlds: mod­est co­er­cion in India be­fore the Emergency, ter­ri­ble co­er­cion dur­ing it, and China’s one-child pol­icy. The more con­cen­trated the power, he ar­gued, the fur­ther a mis­taken idea es­ca­lates into dis­as­ter.
## Fear the bust

Then Shah, whose PhD the­sis was on fer­til­ity, turned the de­bate around. The dan­ger, he ar­gued, is not a boom but a bust. Tyranny breeds hope­less­ness, and peo­ple re­spond by hav­ing fewer chil­dren. {020-C10}
“Having a child is an act of hope,” he said. Russia, which he es­ti­mated has lost about 1.3 mil­lion peo­ple to the war in Ukraine and to em­i­gra­tion, shows the pat­tern today.
The US and the UK had gen­er­a­tions to ad­just to slowly fall­ing fer­til­ity. In China and Russia the chil­dren van­ished sud­denly, leav­ing few young peo­ple to care for many old ones.

India, Shah warned, may be head­ing the same way. Its last cen­sus was in 2011, but other sources point to a rapid fall in fer­til­ity over 10 to 15 years, as would-be par­ents face cramped homes, long com­mutes and poor job prospects. {020-C13}
Varma added an image from a friend’s trav­els in Bihar: streets of idle young men, wait­ing for noth­ing. Without jobs, he said, the de­mo­graphic div­i­dend be­comes a de­mo­graphic dis­as­ter.
The hosts ended with two books writ­ten long ago about the present: Shah’s pick, Hannah Arendt’s *The Origins of Totalitarianism*, and Varma’s, Irawati Karve’s *Yuganta*.

second.label: Economists’ letters
second.head: I told you so, by post
second.deck: Julian Simon’s fix for overbooked flights, and Milton Friedman’s gracious concession

pic.caption: Milton Friedman in New York in 1986

body: In December 1976 a young Julian Simon wrote to Milton Friedman about over­booked flights. Passengers would write sealed bids for the least they would ac­cept to take the next flight; the low­est bid­ders would be paid to wait. {#bid}

Friedman agreed the plan made sense, but would not vouch for it to the Civil Aeronautics Board. If it were that good, he rea­soned, air­lines would al­ready be doing it. Then an econ­o­mist, Alfred E. Kahn, took charge of the board, and the air­lines adopted it. {020-J09}

In 1979 Simon sent Friedman American Airlines’ glow­ing re­port on the scheme. Friedman’s reply was short and gra­cious, and Amit Varma loved it: great peo­ple in di­a­logue, with no ego in­volved. {020-S08}

quote.text: Many thanks for your I told you so, you are en­ti­tled to it.

third.head: Standing room only

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the idle young men of Bihar

body: Amit Varma’s friend Kumar Anand lives in Saharsa, in Bihar. Travelling through semi-urban Bihar near the town, he saw streets full of young men, stand­ing. {020-S07}

They were not wait­ing for a bus, Varma said, or smok­ing at a katta, or wait­ing for a contractor’s truck to take them to work. “They’re just stand­ing. They’re just idle,” he said. It was a haunt­ing image.
Kumar Anand and Mohit Satyanand later took a road trip through Bihar for Varma’s pod­cast, *The Seen and the Unseen*. Much of what they found was young peo­ple who had no jobs, or no longer cared.
“What kids are you gonna have?” Varma asked. Without jobs, he con­cluded later, the de­mo­graphic div­i­dend be­comes a de­mo­graphic dis­as­ter. {#dividend}

p2.title: In defence of people
p2.deck: Amit Varma on a history of population panic, Ajay Shah on why the real danger is a bust {020-C11}

quote.text: More peo­ple mean greater net­works, more pos­i­tive sum games, more dou­ble thank you mo­ments.

photo.caption: Julian Lincoln Simon in academic robes in 1998

box.title: Simon’s big idea
box.text: Julian Simon’s *The Ultimate Resource*, which Amit Varma said came out in 1981 and has a sec­ond edi­tion, ar­gues that human be­ings are the ul­ti­mate re­source. Its the­sis is the root of the episode’s claim that peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs. {020-R02}

sections.label: The premise
sections.head: Brains, not stomachs
sections.caption: people as brains, not stomachs
body: Amit Varma had wanted to make this case for a long time. He began with a 2007 study, Nicholas Eberstadt’s *Too Many People?*, which found no cor­re­la­tion be­tween pop­u­la­tion den­sity and poverty. Monaco is forty times as dense as Bangladesh and far richer; Bahrain is three times as dense as India and far richer. {#monaco}

You don’t even need the data, he said, only com­mon sense. If den­sity made peo­ple poor, they would flee it. Instead, “the whole story of hu­man­ity, all of human his­tory, is about mi­grat­ing from sparsely pop­u­lated rural areas to cities with dense pop­u­la­tions.” {020-C02}
## The ul­ti­mate re­source
His motto, peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs, echoes the econ­o­mist Julian Simon, whose *The Ultimate Resource* ar­gues that human be­ings are the ul­ti­mate re­source. {020-R02}

Simon’s last book, *The Great Breakthrough and Its Cause*, fin­ished by Timur Kuran, goes fur­ther: the in­dus­trial rev­o­lu­tion and pro­duc­tiv­ity booms hap­pened be­cause pop­u­la­tion rose. More peo­ple mul­ti­ply the chances to trade, and ev­ery­one ben­e­fits. {#kuran}
Varma then chal­lenged the viewer. If you are watch­ing in a city, why are you there? If you are in a vil­lage, he said, ei­ther you made your money in a city or you want to go to one.
~ Ask your­self, he said: “Would you say you’re a bur­den on the planet, or would you say that you’re con­tribut­ing some­thing to it?”

quote.text: More peo­ple mean greater net­works, more pos­i­tive sum games, more dou­ble thank you mo­ments.

sections.label: The history
sections.head: Bombs, quotas and bullets
sections.caption: the horrors of population control
body: The idea that peo­ple are a bur­den goes back to 1798, when Thomas Robert Malthus ar­gued that re­sources grow arith­meti­cally while peo­ple grow ex­po­nen­tially. {020-R05}

Amit Varma traced it through Harrison Brown, who com­pared hu­man­ity to mag­gots on a dead cow and backed forcible ster­il­i­sa­tion, to Paul Ehrlich’s 1967 *The Population Bomb*, which an­nounced that “the bat­tle to feed all of hu­man­ity is over.” {020-R06}

The panic be­came pol­icy world­wide. Charles Mann records health work­ers paid by the num­ber of IUDs they in­serted, and birth-control pills pitched out of he­li­copters over vil­lages in the Philippines. {020-R07}
## Quotas from the top

In India, Varma read from Coomi Kapoor’s *The Emergency*. Sanjay Gandhi by­passed the nodal min­istry and went straight to chief min­is­ters eager to please him. Sterilisations rose from 26.24 lakh in 1975-76 to 81.32 lakh in 1976-77, and Haryana hit four times its tar­get. {#lakh}

Every dis­trict and of­fi­cer had quo­tas. Teachers had to “mo­ti­vate” at least five ster­il­i­sa­tions to be paid. Some Delhi gov­ern­ment hos­pi­tals re­fused treat­ment until the pa­tient agreed to be ster­ilised.
~ Even today, Varma said, in­cen­tives are given to doc­tors across rural India to pro­duce ster­il­i­sa­tions, and it is al­ways the women who suf­fer. {#incentives}

quote.text: Some des­per­ate teach­ers were so fran­tic to meet their quo­tas that they of­fered half their salaries to per­suade vol­un­teers to un­dergo the op­er­a­tion.
quote.who: Coomi Kapoor, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The city
sections.head: Twenty minutes from greatness
sections.caption: the greatness of cities
body: Ajay Shah built his in­tu­ition from cities. In *Triumph of the City*, Edward Glaeser ex­plains that cities are great be­cause they pack large num­bers of clever peo­ple close to­gether. {020-R11}

“It’s the num­ber of peo­ple that live within 20 min­utes of you,” Shah said. {020-C03} Their com­bined human cap­i­tal chal­lenges and drives you: we are each crea­tures of the peo­ple around us. Scatter ev­ery­one on a grid 100 me­tres apart, and that flow­er­ing dies.
Modern cul­ture, he ar­gued, is urban, made in dense col­lec­tions of peo­ple, not in the landowner’s machismo of rural life.
## Not des­tiny, but gov­er­nance
Glaeser also shows that dense cities can be ter­ri­ble, with crime, slums and trou­bles of pub­lic health. New York in the 1970s, Shah said, was fa­mous for crime, rats and cock­roaches.

Amit Varma added a les­son from Bjørn Lomborg’s *The Skeptical Environmentalist*: around the turn of the 19th cen­tury, London was as pol­luted as any Indian city today, and it later grew much cleaner. {020-R12}

Nothing about that arc is in­evitable, Shah cau­tioned: it takes pur­pose­ful human ac­tion. But pub­lic health and urban plan­ning for trans­port and parks, he said, are solv­able prob­lems. {020-C04}
~ Even a Mumbai slum, the hosts agreed, is bet­ter than a vil­lage: peo­ple are vot­ing with their feet.

quote.text: These are not be­yond the wit of man, and these are solv­able prob­lems.

sections.label: The state
sections.head: No ceiling on coercion
sections.caption: degrees of coercion
body: Ajay Shah com­pared three worlds of fam­ily plan­ning: pre-Emergency India, with mod­est co­er­cion; Emergency India, sub­ject to the whims of one or two peo­ple; and China under the one-child pol­icy, “Draconian be­yond be­lief”. {020-C07}

The les­son, he said, is about con­cen­trated power: when no­body dares tell the dic­ta­tor he is wrong, ter­ri­ble ideas take hold. The an­swer is to dis­perse power and make such in­tru­sion il­le­git­i­mate.

A gov­ern­ment that tried to stop him hav­ing chil­dren would be creepy, Shah said: “I have no chil­dren today, but that’s my god­damn birthright.” {020-C08} Coercion also comes in de­grees. Stopping a Punjab farmer from burn­ing his field is mild; telling a sin­gle woman she can­not use sur­ro­gacy is “a dif­fer­ent level of evil al­to­gether”.
## The miss­ing brake

Spending, Shah ar­gued, has a built-in brake. Taxes are hard to ex­tract: peo­ple rebel, move their money abroad, dig holes and hide their wealth. So even a half-witted gov­ern­ment weighs what it spends.
Coercion has no such limit. Governments pile one rule on an­other, with no cap on the total and no fine sense of de­gree. “There’s no bud­get con­straint in co­er­cion,” he said. {020-C09}
~ Citizens, he con­cluded, must rebel far more against in­tru­sive co­er­cion. Questions about hav­ing chil­dren should be “the bloody busi­ness of in­di­vid­u­als”.

quote.text: Many ter­ri­ble ideas be­come ac­cepted be­cause no­body has the guts to tell the dic­ta­tor that you’re full of it.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on degrees of coercion

sections.label: The bust
sections.head: When the cradles empty
sections.caption: the danger of a population bust
body: Having a child, Ajay Shah ar­gued, is an act of hope. Drawing on Hannah Arendt, he said tyranny breeds hope­less­ness and stag­na­tion, and men and women re­spond by going on strike. {020-C10}

Russia shows it today. About 300,000 men of re­pro­duc­tive age have died in Ukraine, he es­ti­mated, and about a mil­lion of the best and bright­est have left, tak­ing a fu­ture stream of chil­dren with them. {#russia}
## The arith­metic of age
The real dan­ger, then, is not a boom but a bust. The US and UK de­clined slowly, giv­ing so­ci­ety gen­er­a­tions to ad­just. In China and Russia, the chil­dren van­ished sud­denly. {020-C11}

Set money aside, Shah said, and look only at peo­ple. The old need nurs­ing, cook­ing and clean­ing, which only the young can pro­vide. If ten old peo­ple need fif­teen young ones, that works. If they need sixty, it can­not, and the price of those ser­vices heads to­wards in­fin­ity. {020-C12}

India, he warned, may be next. Other sources point to a rapid fall in fer­til­ity, as would-be par­ents face cramped homes, long com­mutes, a skewed sex ratio and a rule that young peo­ple need a job be­fore mar­riage, when jobs are scarce. {020-C13}
~ Amit Varma saw a vi­cious cir­cle: lose hope, have fewer chil­dren, grow older, and find still less cause for hope.

quote.text: And far from the fears of a pop­u­la­tion bomb. Today we un­der­stand the dam­age from a pop­u­la­tion bust.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the danger of a population bust

quote.text: Do they see jobs? Do they see free­dom? Do they see safety? Or do they see a grim, trou­bled world where there is so­cial strife, an ever-interfering state, and poor eco­nomic prospects?

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A siege, a taxi ride, a wager and a birth strike

stories.kicker: Amit Varma reads Coomi Kapoor on a village under siege
stories.head: The night they came for Pipli
body: Pipli is a vil­lage in Haryana, 45 kilo­me­tres north of Delhi. During the Emergency it be­came the epi­cen­tre of a major riot, Amit Varma said, read­ing from Coomi Kapoor’s *The Emergency*.
It began with a wid­ower, Hawa Singh, who had been forcibly taken for ster­il­i­sa­tion. His in­ci­sion turned sep­tic, his wound fes­tered, and he bled to death.

The block de­vel­op­ment of­fi­cer was un­re­lent­ing. He came back de­mand­ing more vol­un­teers, and had a man re­pair­ing shoes by the road­side picked up. Furious, the vil­lagers drove the of­fi­cer and his men out after a scuf­fle.

Retaliation was swift and bru­tal. Several hun­dred po­lice­men ar­rived, or­dered the men out of their homes and laid siege to the vil­lage through the night. At 6 am shots were fired, and two women mak­ing cow-dung cakes out­side their huts were mowed down.

A warn­ing fol­lowed: if the vil­lagers did not come out, an air­craft would be sent to bomb the whole area. The men sur­ren­dered. Out of a pop­u­la­tion of 2,761, be­tween 400 and 500 were rounded up and ster­ilised. {#pipli}

For Varma, the deeper hor­ror is the mes­sage. Even if you be­lieve pop­u­la­tion is a prob­lem, he said, the state is telling its cit­i­zens that “you do not own your bod­ies”, which is worse than slav­ery. And yet it was nor­malised. {020-S04}
~ Pipli was not alone. Between August and December 1976, Kapoor writes, po­lice opened fire at least eight times on peo­ple re­sist­ing the drive. In three towns alone, twelve peo­ple died. {#firing}
stories.why: Once a pol­icy be­comes a num­ber passed down a hi­er­ar­chy, every link in the chain has a rea­son to co­erce the next. The cru­elty came from the de­sign of the in­cen­tives, not a few bad ap­ples. {020-S03}
stories.postscript: Kapoor, Varma said, is a great jour­nal­ist, and she has also been a guest on his pod­cast *The Seen and the Unseen*.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the siege of Pipli

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the Delhi ride behind a population panic
stories.head: Fleas, dust and a doomsday book
body: Paul Ehrlich wrote that he came to un­der­stand the pop­u­la­tion ex­plo­sion emo­tion­ally one stink­ing hot day in Delhi. {#taxi} In an an­cient taxi hop­ping with fleas, he and his fam­ily crawled through a crowded slum in heat well over a hun­dred de­grees.
He saw “peo­ple, peo­ple, peo­ple, peo­ple”, and won­dered whether they would ever reach their hotel. “And I’m pleased to re­port he did get to his hotel,” Amit Varma said. {020-J03}

Ehrlich also wrote that he could not see how India could feed 200 mil­lion more peo­ple by 1980. {#feed} Since that ride, Varma said, Delhi’s pop­u­la­tion has grown five times, though in the mid-sixties the city was not that crowded. Ehrlich, he said, was “clearly lying”. {020-S02}
~ Such fore­casts, Varma said, came from ex­trap­o­lat­ing fig­ures: at one point Ehrlich imag­ined 70 bil­lion peo­ple vis­it­ing each other by el­e­va­tor, be­cause there would be no roads.
stories.why: The era’s most in­flu­en­tial pop­u­la­tion panic rested on a re­coil from crowds of poor peo­ple, not on ev­i­dence. The city that hor­ri­fied Ehrlich went on to ab­sorb many times more peo­ple. {020-S02}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Paul Ehrlich’s taxi ride

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a bet that put a prophecy to the test
stories.head: Ehrlich bets, Simon collects
body: In the 1970s, Paul Ehrlich re­marked that if he were a gam­bler, he would take even money that England would not exist in the year 2000. {020-S05}

The econ­o­mist Julian Simon no­ticed the word “bet” and, very pub­licly, took him up on it. Ehrlich could choose five re­sources and any pe­riod longer than a year. Simon would wager, Amit Varma thought about $10,000, that their prices would fall.
Ehrlich chose cop­per, chromium, nickel, tin and tung­sten. The bet was made in 1980. By 1990 the prices of all five had fallen, as any­one who knows Econ 101 would ex­pect, Varma said. {#ninety}
~ Yet Ehrlich re­mains a major fig­ure, his ar­ti­cles still ap­pear­ing in big news­pa­pers abroad. “Paul Ehrlich, by the way, is a hero of the left even today,” Varma said.
stories.why: Putting money on a prophecy ex­poses it to re­al­ity. Scarcity sets off in­ge­nu­ity and price ad­just­ment, so re­sources do not sim­ply run out as peo­ple mul­ti­ply. Being wrong, though, rarely costs a pub­lic in­tel­lec­tual his stand­ing.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Simon–Ehrlich wager

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a favourite tale from his PhD reading
stories.head: Between two bad neighbours
body: Ajay Shah had “an amus­ing fact” to share: his PhD the­sis was on fer­til­ity, about women in Malaysia hav­ing ba­bies, which sent him deep into the fer­til­ity lit­er­a­ture. {020-S06}
His favourite story from it is Poland. A young coun­try born out of the Treaty of Versailles, it was in­vaded by the Soviets al­most at once, and Leon Trotsky was stopped at its edges.

Then came a pre­car­i­ous life be­tween Germany and the Soviet Union, both, Shah said, ter­ri­ble neigh­bours to have. So birth rates col­lapsed, with no mod­ern re­pro­duc­tive tech­nol­ogy. “When hope dies, you stop hav­ing chil­dren,” Shah said. {#hope}
~ To have chil­dren, he said, you need to be in a cer­tain place, in your heart and in your sense of the world: “What kind of world are we going to bring our chil­dren into?”
stories.why: Fertility tracks how peo­ple see the fu­ture. Fear alone, under hos­tile neigh­bours or a tyrant, can make a so­ci­ety stop hav­ing chil­dren, with no pill re­quired. Shah sees the same pat­tern in Russia today. {#russia}

quiz.q: Which five metals did Paul Ehrlich pick for his wager with Julian Simon?
quiz.a: Copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tung­sten, and all five were cheaper by 1990.

quiz.q: According to Nicholas Eberstadt’s study, how does Monaco compare with Bangladesh?
quiz.a: It has forty times the pop­u­la­tion den­sity, and is far richer.

quiz.q: Why did Thomas Robert Malthus, writing in 1798, think mass starvation was inevitable?
quiz.a: People grow ex­po­nen­tially while re­sources grow only arith­meti­cally, so re­sources would run out.

quiz.q: What was the subject of Ajay Shah’s PhD thesis, his “amusing fact”?
quiz.a: Fertility, specif­i­cally women in Malaysia hav­ing ba­bies, which took him into the lit­er­a­ture.

quiz.q: In an ageing society, why do personal services for the elderly become unaffordable?
quiz.a: Only the young can pro­vide them and they can’t be im­ported, so prices soar.

quiz.q: During the Emergency, what did government teachers have to do to be paid?
quiz.a: Motivate at least five ster­il­i­sa­tions; some of­fered half their salaries to find vol­un­teers.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 20. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Paul R. Ehrlich (Ilka Hartmann, public domain); Julian Simon (Manuel Castells, CC BY-SA 2.0); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain); Thomas Robert Malthus (John Linnell, CC BY 4.0); Hannah Arendt (Wikimedia Commons, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Open Library and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: Population Is Not a Problem, but Our Greatest Strength
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s chal­lenge to the school les­son that pop­u­la­tion is India’s big­gest prob­lem: peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs, pop­u­la­tion den­sity drives pros­per­ity, and the ills blamed on pop­u­la­tion are fail­ures of gov­er­nance.

shelf.title: The Ultimate Resource
shelf.creator: Julian Simon
shelf.why: Its the­sis that human be­ings are the ul­ti­mate re­source is the root of the ‘peo­ple are brains, not stomachs’ world­view.

shelf.title: Too Many People?
shelf.creator: Nicholas Eberstadt
shelf.why: It finds no cor­re­la­tion be­tween pop­u­la­tion den­sity and poverty, with strik­ing coun­terex­am­ples: Monaco is forty times as dense as Bangladesh and far richer, and Bahrain is three times as dense as India and far richer.

shelf.title: The Great Breakthrough and Its Cause
shelf.creator: Julian Simon
shelf.why: It ex­tends Simon’s ar­gu­ment that the in­dus­trial rev­o­lu­tion and pro­duc­tiv­ity booms hap­pened be­cause pop­u­la­tion rose.

shelf.title: An Essay on the Principle of Population
shelf.creator: Thomas Robert Malthus
shelf.why: Read it to see where the idea began: Malthus claimed peo­ple grow ex­po­nen­tially while re­sources grow arith­meti­cally, so mass star­va­tion was in­evitable.

shelf.title: The Population Bomb
shelf.creator: Paul Ehrlich
shelf.why: A case study in con­fi­dent doom.

shelf.title: The Book That Incited a Worldwide Fear of Overpopulation
shelf.creator: Charles Mann
shelf.why: It shows the global scale of the co­er­cion: health work­ers paid per IUD in­serted, birth-control pills pitched out of he­li­copters over vil­lages in the Philippines, and mil­lions ster­ilised, often co­er­cively, from Mexico to Bangladesh.

shelf.title: The Emergency: A Personal History
shelf.creator: Coomi Kapoor
shelf.why: A journalist’s first-hand ac­count of the Emergency, when half the op­po­si­tion and hordes of jour­nal­ists were jailed and a ster­il­i­sa­tion drive spun out of con­trol.

shelf.title: Coomi Kapoor Has the Inside Track (Episode 305 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A long con­ver­sa­tion with Coomi Kapoor, whose first-hand ac­count of the Emergency Amit re­lies on; a com­pan­ion to her book The Emergency: A Personal History.

shelf.title: The Simon–Ehrlich wager
shelf.why: Background on the 1980 wager in which all five met­als Ehrlich chose (cop­per, chromium, nickel, tin and tung­sten) were cheaper by 1990.

shelf.title: Triumph of the City
shelf.creator: Edward Glaeser
shelf.why: Glaeser ex­plains that cities are great be­cause they pack clever peo­ple close to­gether, while ad­mit­ting dense cities can be ter­ri­ble (crime, slums, pub­lic health), which makes good gov­er­nance the real chal­lenge.

shelf.title: The Skeptical Environmentalist
shelf.creator: Bjørn Lomborg
shelf.why: Lomborg traces how great Western cities like London, once as filthy and un­healthy as any Indian city today, cleaned up as they got richer.

shelf.title: The Origins of Totalitarianism
shelf.creator: Hannah Arendt
shelf.why: Arendt was among the first to show how much Nazi Germany and Stalin’s Russia had in com­mon, which makes her an es­sen­tial guide to au­thor­i­tar­ian regimes.

shelf.title: Yuganta
shelf.creator: Irawati Karve
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite books: a bril­liant, some­times dis­qui­et­ing so­ci­o­log­i­cal read­ing of the Mahabharata and the role of women in it, can­did about its misog­yny, and an anal­y­sis of a so­ci­ety we still live in.

shelf.title: What Bruce Springsteen Means to Us (Episode 13)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A labour of love about the mu­si­cian who mat­ters to both hosts, which Amit calls the show’s least-watched episode.

shelf.title: The State of the Ukraine War (Episode 14)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mil­i­tary-strategy anal­y­sis of the war: how it is chang­ing the way wars are fought, Ukrainian in­no­va­tion, and its de­mo­graphic toll on Russia, from deaths to the flight of a mil­lion of its best and bright­est.

shelf.title: Understanding Baumol’s Cost Disease And Its Impact On Healthcare
shelf.creator: Varun Ganapathi
shelf.why: He calls it ‘one of those great ideas in eco­nom­ics.’ It bears di­rectly on his point that per­sonal ser­vices for the el­derly, which only young peo­ple can pro­vide, be­come un­af­ford­able when the young are scarce.

shelf.title: The Evil of Family Planning
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: His ear­lier case that ster­il­i­sa­tion camps and in­cen­tives still op­er­ate in India today, long after the Emergency.

shelf.title: Economic Learnings of India for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Bihar (Episode 345 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s guests on Bihar de­scribe both the in­ven­tive things hap­pen­ing there, ev­i­dence of India’s un­tapped po­ten­tial, and young peo­ple with­out jobs who have lost hope: the human face of a de­mo­graphic div­i­dend turn­ing into a dis­as­ter.

shelf.title: The Effect of Age-Specific Sex Ratios on Crime: Instrumental Variable Estimates from India
shelf.creator: Rashmi Barua, Prarthna Goel and Renuka Sane
shelf.why: Using an in­ter­est­ing iden­ti­fi­ca­tion strat­egy, it finds that when the sex ratio tilts to­ward ex­cess males, crime rises.

laughs.text: Noticing that the hosts are wear­ing match­ing shirts, Ajay asks: ‘What spon­ta­neous ban­ter can we do about this spon­ta­neous order?’

Amit says the de­sign on Ajay’s shirt re­minds him of ‘mag­gots on a dead cow,’ then re­veals the source: twen­ti­eth-century pop­u­la­tion pes­simist Harrison Brown, who wrote that hu­man­ity ‘will not rest con­tent until the earth is cov­ered com­pletely and to a con­sid­er­able depth with a writhing mass of human be­ings, much as a dead cow is cov­ered with a pul­sat­ing mass of mag­gots.’

After read­ing Ehrlich’s an­guished ‘Would we ever get to our hotel?’, Amit dead­pans: ‘And I’m pleased to re­port he did get to his hotel.’ Later he adds that Ehrlich is still a hero of the left even though ‘he has been wrong about ev­ery­thing in his life.’

Ajay on botched ster­il­i­sa­tion camps: ‘the au­to­clave will not be work­ing, the in­stru­ments will be con­tam­i­nated. That’s gar­den va­ri­ety in­com­pe­tence of the Indian state. That’s un­sur­pris­ing.’

Ajay on India’s sta­tis­tics: ‘The bad news to you, Virginia, if you be­lieved that the Indian cen­sus was gospel truth. It’s not.’ He adds that Indian-style ger­ry­man­der­ing works by ma­nip­u­lat­ing the cen­sus rather than by re­draw­ing con­stituen­cies.
Amit: ‘I some­times provoca­tively say that most Urdu po­etry is a whin­ing of in­cels, but you know, that is just a provo­ca­tion, but the whin­ing of in­cels could kinda be­come a prob­lem.’

Julian Simon’s gloat-without-gloating let­ter to Milton Friedman: ‘I’m one of your great fans, and I’m not an I told you so type. Still, you may find it in­ter­est­ing to com­pare your sec­ond and third para­graphs...’

Amit on Alfred E. Kahn, the econ­o­mist whose ap­point­ment to the Civil Aeronautics Board let Simon’s over­book­ing auc­tion hap­pen: ‘he’s a good econ­o­mist be­cause not all econ­o­mists get eco­nom­ics, but he’s a good econ­o­mist. He gets it.’
‘Hum Do Hamare Do’ (‘We two, our two’), the fam­ily-planning slo­gan Amit grew up with and the ca­nard he wants to dis­man­tle.

Malthus’s no­to­ri­ous line from his 1798 essay: ‘Instead of rec­om­mend­ing clean­li­ness to the poor, we should en­cour­age con­trary habits and court the re­turn of the plague,’ be­cause for him the plague would be de­liv­er­ance.

Robert Sapolsky, prob­a­bly on an episode of Sam Harris’s pod­cast (‘I might be misremembering’), is Amit’s source for the claim that the so­cial­is­ing part of the male brain ma­tures only around 25.
